extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent practitioners advising on written description compliance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application’s specification and related disclosure demonstrate that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description). Covers claim construction, support for claim elements, means-plus-function, species/genus distinctions, and art-specific considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is an essential part of the examination process. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire claim must be considered, including preamble language and the transitional phrase. The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble. See cases cited (e.g., In re Katz, In re Morris, Lockwood). Do not import limitations into the claims from the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat preamble and transitional phrases appropriately (comprising/consisting essentially of/consisting of)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble language and the transitional term must be given proper import; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' signals limited openness, and 'consisting of' is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Comprising’ covers the recited subject matter alone or with unrecited subject matter. 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground; absent clear indication in spec/claims of what basic and novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising.' If applicant contends additional elements are excluded by 'consisting essentially of,' applicant bears the burden of showing additional elements would materially change the invention. (See Genentech v. Chiron; PPG Indus.; AK Steel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the entire application to find support for claimed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to determining whether the disclosure provides adequate written description for the claimed subject matter, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification, including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review should include summary, detailed description, claims, abstract, drawings, sequence listings. Determine the field of the invention and the level of skill and knowledge in the art; consider what a person of ordinary skill would understand from the disclosure at the filing date (see Wang Labs.). Information well known in the art need not be described in detail (Hybritech). Use patents and publications to assess maturity of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requires showing possession of the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there is sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown in many ways: reduction to practice, detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas, or any description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics such that a skilled artisan recognizes applicant had possession. The inquiry is factual and case-by-case (Purdue Pharma; Pfaff v. Wells).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice can show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention (constructing an embodiment or performing a process that met all claim limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice requires a physical embodiment including all limitations and a determination that the invention will work for its intended purpose (Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder). For biological materials, description of a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may evidence reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas can show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or in structural chemical formulas can permit a person skilled in the art to recognize that applicant had possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings alone may provide an adequate written description (Vas-Cath; Wolfensperger; Autogiro). Generic chemical formulae often indicate with specificity what a genus claim encompasses; one skilled in the art can identify many species from a formula (Eli Lilly). The description need only detail what is new or not conventional (Hybritech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying characteristics other than full structure can show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation to structure, method of making) may demonstrate possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, cleavage patterns, restriction maps, enzymatic activities, antibody cross-reactivity. Where a strong correlation between structure and function exists, function plus minimal structure may suffice (Enzo Biochem, Falkner v. Inglis, Capon v. Eshhar). Conversely, describing a composition by function alone typically will not suffice (Eli Lilly; Fiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional disclosure vs structural disclosure — when function alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing a composition or gene by its function alone is typically insufficient to support claims to that composition; an inventor must provide structure, method of obtaining, or other distinguishing characteristics unless a well-established correlation allows prediction of structure from function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: a gene cannot be claimed merely by describing its function (Eli Lilly); disclosure of an antigen does not by itself provide adequate written description of antibodies claimed by binding affinity (Amgen v. Sanofi; Centocor v. Abbott). If the art establishes strong correlation between structure and function, one skilled in the art may predict structure from function with reasonable confidence (Enzo Biochem). Without correlation, function-only disclosure is a 'wish' rather than possession (In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA para 6) require corresponding structure/materials/acts in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must consider summary/detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings to find corresponding structure. Written description adequacy for means-plus-function requires either (1) the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform the recited function, or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know what structure in the specification performs the function. Failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure makes the limitation indefinite under 112(b) and also fails 112(a). See Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino; In re Noll; MPEP §2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a means-/step-plus-function limitation lacks corresponding structure, reject under both indefiniteness and written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) for lack of corresponding structure for a means-plus-function limitation cannot stand where there is adequate description in the specification to satisfy 112(a); conversely, lack of corresponding structure supports rejection under both 112(b) and 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a means-plus-function limitation is indefinite for lack of disclosed corresponding structure/materials/acts, then the claim limitation lacks an adequate written description as well and should be rejected accordingly. See In re Noll and cited guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze single-embodiment/species claims with a stepwise checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims drawn to a single embodiment or species, follow the specific checklist: (A) does the application describe an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, does it include drawings or structural formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, does it set forth distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application as filed describes the complete structure or acts of the claimed invention as a whole, the written description requirement is satisfied. If complete structure is not disclosed, determine whether other identifying characteristics (including function+structure correlation in biotech) allow a skilled artisan to recognize possession. Examples/case law and further sub-steps provided in the guideline (Fields v. Conover; Eli Lilly; In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genus claims from species claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment or species is analyzed as a claim to that species; a claim encompassing two or more embodiments or species is analyzed as a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §806.04(e). The written description expectations differ: genus-level claims require adequate support across the breadth, while species claims are judged against the single disclosed embodiment/species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider factors affecting sufficiency of written description (art maturity, skill level, method of making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination considering multiple factors: level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with correlation, and method of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature. In mature technologies where knowledge and skill are high, written description questions are less likely for claims present in the original filing, even when only a method of making is disclosed. In emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required. Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization may be insufficient (Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process vs product claims — process disclosure may not support product claim absent evidence product is produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim (other than a product-by-process claim). If the process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for a product-by-process claim is satisfied; otherwise the requirement may not be met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen. Where it is not clear that the acts in the specification can be performed or that the product is produced by the process, written description may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is conventional or well known need not be disclosed in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Information well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be described in detail in the specification for purposes of written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply in context of particular invention and state of knowledge (Hybritech; Capon v. Eshhar). The balance between what must be disclosed and what is known shifts as the field evolves.
